entries.name: Dromedary camel
entries.migrates: no fixed circuit; nomadic with herders and feral wandering
behaviour: hump stores fat, not water
tolerates water loss over 30% of body mass and drinks 100 litres in minutes
paces with both legs of one side moving together
entries.notes: Extinct in the wild for two millennia: every dromedary is descended from domestic stock. Feral herds in Australia are the closest thing to wild camels left.

entries.name: Arabian oryx
behaviour: digs shallow depressions under shade to rest
both sexes carry long straight horns
herds rest in the open and feed at dawn and dusk

voxel_model.pattern: dark flank stripe, dark leg and face markings

entries.notes: Extinct in the wild by 1972, saved in zoos and reintroduced across Oman, Jordan, Saudi Arabia and the UAE. The white silhouette of the Arabian desert.

entries.name: Addax
behaviour: broad splayed hooves for loose sand
winter coat darkens from near-white to grey-brown
rests in scrapes in the heat of the day

voxel_model.pattern: pale body, dark forelock fringe and twisted horns

entries.notes: Critically endangered: only a few hundred survive in Chad and Niger. Reintroduction programmes are under way; never treat it as spawnable game.

entries.name: Dorcas gazelle
behaviour: never needs to drink; moisture from browse
stands on hind legs to reach acacia foliage
stotting leaps when alarmed

voxel_model.pattern: faint flank stripe, lyre-shaped horns on both sexes

entries.notes: The archetypal small desert gazelle of North Africa; can go its whole life without a drink.

entries.name: Dama gazelle
entries.migrates: follows rain across the Sahel-Sahara edge
behaviour: long lyre-shaped horns in both sexes
large social herds on open flat ground
seasonal movements tracked by rain

voxel_model.pattern: rufous upperparts, white legs and rump, dark neck patch

entries.notes: Critically endangered; only around 200 persist in the wild, all in the Sahel belt. A ghost of the great Saharan herds.

entries.name: Arabian sand gazelle (rhim)
behaviour: pale sand-toned coat nearly invisible on dunes
lives on loose dunes and gravel plains
forages dawn and dusk, shade at noon
entries.notes: The rhim of Arabia and Iraq; extinct across much of its former range and back only through fenced reintroduction herds.

entries.name: Desert bighorn sheep
entries.migrates: elevational, between desert ranges and high forage
behaviour: clings to near-vertical rock faces
rams clash in rutting head-butting duels
tied to scattered desert water holes
entries.notes: Icon of the American canyon country; isolated ranges mean each herd is its own genetic island.

entries.name: Nubian ibex
behaviour: impossible climbing on sheer cliff bands
males fight with huge backward-curving ridged horns
haunts rocky wadis and cliff bases

voxel_model.pattern: ridged scimitar horns, dark dorsal stripe

entries.notes: The cliff goat of the Sinai, Arabia and the Red Sea hills; a fixture of wadi scenes and cliff faces.

entries.name: Red kangaroo
behaviour: largest living marsupial; males red, females blue-grey
embryonic diapause: embryo waits while previous joey in pouch
boxing duels between males
entries.notes: Emblem of the Australian outback; mobs linger near water and mob-jump with huge bounding leaps.

entries.name: Emu
behaviour: males incubate the nest alone for ~8 weeks and lose a third of their body weight
pairs stride across open country in single file
booming infrasound carries far at dawn
entries.notes: Second-largest living bird; the male alone broods a nest of huge dark eggs. gestation_days is incubation time.

entries.name: Greater bilby
behaviour: long pink rabbit-like ears and a crested blue-grey rump
digs spiral burrows several metres long
pouch opens backward so dirt stays out while digging

voxel_model.pattern: crested rump, dark and white banded tail

entries.notes: Endangered; survival now depends on feral-free reserves and breeding centres. The Australian desert's little rabbit-eared digger.

entries.name: Spinifex hopping mouse
behaviour: huge kangaroo-rat ears; hears beetles under spinifex
never drinks; metabolic water from seeds
digs spiral burrows under spinifex hummocks
entries.notes: The classic never-drinking mouse of the red sand; a two-block silhouette with ears bigger than its body.

entries.name: Gila monster
behaviour: one of only two venomous lizards in the world
stores fat in its bulbous tail for lean months
slow, deliberate walk; venom delivered by chewing
entries.notes: Beaded venomous lizard of the Sonoran and Mojave; protected across its range. A slow, heavy-tailed boss-adjacent encounter.

entries.name: Mojave desert tortoise
behaviour: digs burrows several metres long to escape heat
drinks from temporary rain pools, sometimes quartered by many tortoises at once
adults can outlive most other reptiles in the region
entries.notes: Threatened; lives longer than its keeper's grandparents. Juvenile tortoises are heavily preyed on by ravens.

entries.name: Sidewinder rattlesnake
behaviour: moves sideways across loose dunes leaving J-shaped tracks
horn-like supraocular scales over the eyes
lies buried under sand with only the eyes exposed
entries.notes: The dune rattler; the sidewinding track in sand is a giveaway for players exploring dune biomes.

entries.name: Horned viper
behaviour: sidewinds across dunes, buried in seconds
paired supraocular horn scales like tiny horns over the eyes
ambushes at night from beneath the sand

voxel_model.pattern: pale sandy blotches, horn scales over the eyes

entries.notes: The sidewinder of the Sahara and Arabia; sister in behavior to its North American cousin. Tracks show the same sidewind signature.

entries.name: Sandfish skink
behaviour: swims through loose sand with fringed shovel-snout
dives and vanishes in under a second when alarmed
digs to escape both heat and predators
entries.notes: The fish of the dunes; it appears to swim through sand and is one of the strangest small lizards to encounter on a dune crest.

entries.name: Chuckwalla
behaviour: inflates its body into rock crevices so it cannot be pulled out
basks boldly on boulders above the heat shimmer
bolts into cracks at the first shadow

voxel_model.pattern: dark with orange-red face in old males

entries.notes: Big-bodied rock-crevice lizard of the Sonoran-Mojave lava fields; impossible to extract from its crack hideout once wedged in.

entries.name: Egyptian spiny-tailed lizard (dhub)
behaviour: thick flattened tail covered in spiny ridged scales
digs long burrows and sun-basks at the entrance
strictly plant-eating; fat stored in the tail
entries.notes: The dhub of Arabia and Egypt; eaten locally but now protected in much of its range. Spiny tail is the giveaway at distance.

entries.name: Thorny devil
behaviour: skin grooves channel dew and water to its mouth
sits motionless over ant trails and licks them up
false head-spike on the neck to misdirect strikes
entries.notes: Living landmine of spikes that drinks through its skin. Walks with a stiff, rocking gait that sells the model.

entries.name: Perentie
behaviour: largest lizard in Australia
rears up tripoded on tail and forelimbs when cornered
raids burrows, nests and carcasses alike
entries.notes: Australia's monitor giant; an adult perentie is a real mid-game threat in desert blocks.

entries.name: Golden eagle
behaviour: stoop from great height at 200+ km/h
mates soar together in paired cliff-side displays
rides thermals over desert ridges all morning
entries.notes: Top raptor of open desert and canyon country; the huge nest (eyrie) on cliffs is a landmark for desert cliffs. gestation_days is incubation.

entries.name: Greater roadrunner
behaviour: runs down rattlesnakes and thrashes them against rocks
sun-bathes with back feathers flattened to absorb heat
pairs hunt their own territories in silence
entries.notes: The cartoon bird runs like the real thing: a fast, grounded sprint with a crest flashing up. gestation_days is incubation.

entries.name: Burrowing owl
behaviour: lives underground in mammal burrows, standing at the entrance like a sentry
bobs up and down when alarmed
forages close to the ground on long legs
entries.notes: The little ground-standing owl of burrow country; imitates a rattlesnake from inside its burrow. gestation_days is incubation.

entries.name: Houbara bustard (African houbara)
entries.migrates: Asian population migrates to Arabia for winter; African resident
behaviour: male displays by fluffing neck feathers into a ruff
walks with a slow dignified stride
the traditional quarry of Arabian falconry

voxel_model.pattern: fine dark neck stripe and scalloped mottling

entries.notes: Vulnerable and declining across its range, largely from falconry and poaching. gestation_days is incubation. The Asian houbara is now treated as a separate species (C. macqueenii).

entries.name: Double-banded sandgrouse
entries.migrates: daily flights between roost and distant waterholes
behaviour: males soak their belly feathers at the waterhole and fly home to drip water into chicks
flies in flocks to water at dawn and dusk across hundreds of kilometres
swift pigeon-like flight between foraging and water

voxel_model.pattern: double black chest bands, barred flanks

entries.notes: The bird that carries water home in its belly feathers: one of the great avian tricks. gestation_days is incubation.

entries.name: Fennec fox
behaviour: oversized ears radiate heat and hear prey under sand
hairy soles for hot sand; digs deep burrows
pairs mate for life and den together
entries.notes: World's smallest canid; those huge ears are thermal radiators. A delightful small encounter for desert dunes at night.

entries.name: Sand cat
behaviour: flat wide head with low-set ears built for dune-burrow listening
furred paw pads protect against scorching dune sand
digs burrows and bolt-holes into dunes

voxel_model.pattern: faint stripes, black ear-backs and striped tail rings

entries.notes: The only cat that lives deep in true dune fields. Extremely rare and near-invisible; all sightings are precious.

entries.name: Kit fox
behaviour: main prey is the kangaroo rat; hunts by pouncing
year-round dens with multiple entrances
pairs den together and raise pups cooperatively
entries.notes: North America's dune-field fox; the kit fox's night yipping telegraphs its presence before you ever see it.

entries.name: Rüppell's fox
behaviour: banded black-and-silver back as camouflage on stony desert
lives in stone deserts where fennecs cannot
digs multi-entrance dens in gravel and sand

voxel_model.pattern: silvery-silver agouti banding on the back

entries.notes: Fennec's stony-desert cousin; greyer and smaller-eared, equally at home in gravel hamada and erg edge.

entries.name: Egyptian desert hedgehog
behaviour: rolls into a spine-ball and wedges under rocks
eats scorpions, immune to their venom
long hibernation in the coldest months

voxel_model.pattern: white crown band across the forehead

entries.notes: The small spiny ghost of wadis; an immune scorpion-eater. A roly-poly night encounter.

entries.name: Lesser jerboa
behaviour: hops on two feet like a miniature kangaroo
tail used as balance and a fifth limb
zig-zag hopping escape when startled
entries.notes: Four-toed kangaroo of the dunes; a two-block hop-and-freeze silhouette in moonlight.

entries.name: Merriam's kangaroo rat
behaviour: never drinks; extracts water from dry seeds
hops on enlarged hind legs with huge ears
stuffs cheek pouches and hoards seeds in burrows

voxel_model.pattern: dark dorsal stripe, white hip and cheek patches

entries.notes: The seed-hoarding kangaroo rat drives the rodent economy of North American desert scrub.

entries.name: Deathstalker scorpion
behaviour: among the most venomous scorpions alive; dangerous to children
glows blue-green under UV light
digs shallow scrapes under stones in the day
entries.notes: Tiny, fluorescent under ultraviolet light, and one of the nastiest stings in the desert. Handle with care.

entries.name: Desert locust
entries.migrates: gregarious swarms migrate up to 150 km a day
behaviour: transforms between solitary and swarming gregarious phases with crowding
a single large swarm can eat as much in a day as tens of thousands of people
flies with the prevailing winds over 1500 km

voxel_model.pattern: yellow with dark mottling in gregarious phase

entries.notes: When alone a plain grasshopper; when crowded, a Biblical plague. Swarms are a candidate world event, not an ambient mob.

entries.name: Saharan silver ant
behaviour: forages at midday when sand surface hits 70°C and predators flee
silver hairs reflect heat and light like brushed aluminium
races out, grabs heat-killed prey, and is back in the nest in under ten minutes
entries.notes: The hottest-foraging animal on Earth; a glittering comma dashing across sand that would blister a boot.

entries.name: Death's-head hawkmoth
behaviour: skull-like thorax marking
squeaks loudly when handled by vibrating air through its proboscis
raids beehives at night to steal honey, mimicking bee pheromones
entries.notes: The moth of Hannibal Lecter fame: skull-faced, honey-thieving, and it squeaks when grabbed.

entries.name: Desert elephant (Gourma population)
entries.migrates: seasonal transhumance of 500+ km between the Inland Niger Delta and the desert edge
behaviour: only elephants that permanently inhabit open desert
digs wells in soft riverbed sand during dry season
walks hundreds of kilometres between water sources in family groups
entries.notes: Not a subspecies but a population: the Gourma elephants of Mali are the only permanently desert-adapted elephants. Critically threatened by drought and conflict.
